headline: A Berlin Heart Gives Baby Macs a Second Chance at Life
meta_description: After cardiac arrest left baby Macs facing end-of-life care, a mechanical Berlin Heart device has transformed him into a thriving infant waiting for transplant.
summary_short: Baby Macs was given days to live after sudden cardiac arrests. Now fitted with a Berlin Heart device, he's smiling and thriving while awaiting a heart transplant.
body:
When baby Macs Green suffered two sudden cardiac arrests and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, his parents Dylan and Catrin faced an unthinkable choice. Doctors at Bristol Royal Children's Hospital, where Macs lay sedated on life support, asked them to prepare for the worst. But then came an unexpected lifeline: the Berlin Heart, a mechanical device that takes over the pumping function of a failing heart while patients await transplant. Manufactured in Germany, this ventricular assist device works through air power to circulate blood throughout the body. Within weeks of receiving the implant, Macs became unrecognizable to his family—not because of the surgery, but because of what it gave him back. "He's smiling, he's responding to us," Dylan said. "Before, he was just a small baby lying on a bed." His mother echoed the sentiment, describing the transformation as "like having our baby back."

The Berlin Heart has quietly revolutionized pediatric cardiology since the first European patient received one in 1990. By 2014, over 1,500 children and infants had been fitted with the device, which comes in two formats depending on whether one or both sides of the heart need support. A toddler once lived with the device for 2.5 years while awaiting transplant, demonstrating its durability and reliability.

For Macs, the device means he no longer needs the heavy sedation that kept him unconscious and immobile. The change in his quality of life has been immediate and profound. Though no one knows how long he will wait for a donor heart—it could take years—his family now has something they didn't have before: genuine hope and a child who is thriving.
quick_facts: Baby Macs received a Berlin Heart at Bristol Royal Children's Hospital
Device uses air power to mechanically pump blood throughout the body
Over 1,500 Berlin Hearts fitted to children by 2014
One toddler lived with the device for 2.5 years awaiting transplant
